unit.title: Cut, bend and install electrical conduits

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which PPE should you wear when cutting steel conduit with a hacksaw?
options: A dust mask and ear defenders only
A welding helmet and rubber boots
Nothing extra, as hacksaws are hand tools
Safety glasses, and gloves for sharp edges

questions.stem: Why should PVC solvent cement be used only where there is good airflow?
options: So that the joint sets slowly enough to adjust it
So that the cement does not change colour
Its fumes are harmful and can catch fire
So that the conduit stays cool in the sun

questions.stem: How should you heat PVC conduit to bend it?
options: With a gas blowtorch held close to the PVC tube
Over an open fire made from scrap timber
By hitting it with a hammer until it is warm
With a heat gun or heating box, as the maker says

questions.stem: Before you cut any conduit, what should you check on the drawing and on site?
options: The colour of the paint on the ceiling
The route, box positions and lengths
Which worker cut the conduit on the last job
The name of the shop that sold the conduit

questions.stem: Which conduit can be threaded at its ends to take screwed couplings?
options: Heavy-gauge (rigid) steel conduit
Thin-wall steel tubing (EMT)
Light-gauge rigid PVC conduit
Corrugated flexible plastic conduit

questions.stem: How is thin-wall steel tubing (EMT) usually joined?
options: By threading the ends and fitting screwed couplings
With set-screw or compression couplings
With solvent cement, like PVC conduit
By welding the two ends together

questions.stem: Why should you measure twice before cutting conduit?
options: So the tape measure stays accurate for longer
So that you use more conduit on the job
To avoid waste from a length cut wrong
Because the drawing never shows any lengths

questions.stem: How should a hacksaw blade be fitted for cutting conduit?
options: Teeth pointing away from the handle, held tight
Teeth pointing back toward the handle, held loose
Either way round, as long as the blade is sharp
Teeth pointing up, with the blade fitted loosely

questions.stem: When cutting thin-wall conduit with a hacksaw, why use a blade with fine teeth?
options: Fine teeth cut faster than coarse teeth on all metals
Fine teeth make the blade last for ever
Fine teeth stop the tube from getting warm
So at least three teeth touch the thin wall at once

questions.stem: Why must a conduit be cut square (straight across)?
options: So the conduit looks shiny at the end
So that it can be bent more easily later
So the cable can be pulled in faster
So it fits fully into couplings and boxes

questions.stem: Why must the inside of a cut end of conduit be reamed?
options: To remove sharp edges that can cut cables
To make the conduit wall thinner and lighter
To make the conduit bend more easily at the end
To clean off the paint before fitting a saddle

questions.stem: Which tool is used to ream the inside edge of a steel conduit end?
options: A cold chisel and a hammer
A centre punch and mallet
A reamer or half-round file
A spirit level and tape

questions.stem: What should be put on the die when threading steel conduit?
options: Water, to keep the die and conduit cool
Cutting oil, made for threading
Grease, packed thickly into the teeth
Nothing, as the die must be kept dry

questions.stem: While threading conduit with a die stock, why do you turn it back a little every so often?
options: To check that the thread is on the right way
To make the thread longer than needed
To break off and clear the metal chips
To rest your arms between each full turn

questions.stem: What is the right way to make a solvent-cement joint in PVC conduit?
options: Apply cement to the fitting only, then push in slowly
Clean both parts, apply cement, push fully home and hold
Push the parts together dry, then paint cement on the outside
Warm the parts with a flame, then cement them together

questions.stem: Why are expansion couplings fitted in long PVC conduit runs outdoors?
options: PVC grows and shrinks as the temperature changes
They let rain water drain out of the conduit run
They make the conduit run stronger when it is hit
They allow the cables to be joined inside the run

questions.stem: What does a bending spring do when bending PVC conduit?
options: It stops the conduit wall flattening or kinking
It heats the PVC so that it bends more easily
It measures the angle of the bend as you go
It holds the conduit against the wall after bending

questions.stem: When making a cold bend in PVC with a spring, what is good practice?
options: Leave the spring inside the conduit for good
Bend a little past the angle, then ease back
Heat the bend with a lighter to set it
Pull the spring out before the bend is made

questions.stem: Which tool is used to make bends in steel conduit by hand on site?
options: A large pipe wrench
A PVC bending spring
A pair of large pliers
A conduit hand bender

questions.stem: A steel bend has flattened (kinked) on the outside. What should you do?
options: Hammer it round again so it looks better
Use it, because the cable will still fit
Cut it out and make the bend again
Fill the dent with tape and carry on

questions.stem: What is an offset (set) in a conduit run?
options: One single bend made to exactly 90°
A cut made at 45° across the tube
Two bends that step the run to one side
A coupling used where two runs meet

questions.stem: What is a saddle bend used for?
options: To hold the conduit flat against the wall
To take the run over a pipe in its path
To join two lengths of conduit end to end
To turn the run through a full 90° corner

questions.stem: An offset is made with two 30° bends. The offset is 100 mm deep. How far apart should the two bends be?
options: 200 mm
100 mm
141 mm
300 mm

questions.stem: For an offset, the distance between the two bends is the offset depth times a multiplier. What is the multiplier for two 45° bends?
options: About 2.0
About 2.6
About 6.0
About 1.4

questions.stem: In an offset, what happens if you use smaller bend angles, such as 22½° instead of 45°?
options: The bends must be closer together
The cable becomes harder to pull in
The offset can only be made in PVC
The bends must be further apart

questions.stem: Why must the bender maker's marks and take-up figures be followed when bending?
options: So the bender stays clean and does not rust
So the bend lands in the right place on the run
So the conduit can be bent without any force
So the bend can be any angle you like

questions.stem: Why should the total amount of bending between two draw-in points be limited?
options: So the conduit can be painted more easily
So that fewer saddles are needed on the run
So cables can be pulled in without damage
So the conduit run looks shorter on the wall

questions.stem: How should conduit saddles be spaced along a straight run?
options: Evenly, at the spacing the code and drawing give
Only at the two ends of each length of conduit
As far apart as the conduit will allow before sagging
Wherever the wall is easiest to drill

questions.stem: Where else, besides along straight runs, should saddles be fitted?
options: Only in the middle of each bend
Halfway between each coupling only
Nowhere else, as boxes hold the conduit
Close to each box, bend and fitting

questions.stem: Which fixings are suitable for saddles on a concrete block wall?
options: Nails hammered into the mortar joints
Screws into wall plugs in drilled holes
Glue only, pressed on for one minute
Tie wire wrapped around the blocks

questions.stem: Which tool checks that a vertical conduit drop is plumb?
options: A spirit level held against the conduit
A tape measure held along the conduit
A try square set on the floor below it
A pipe wrench on the coupling

questions.stem: What holds a threaded steel conduit end in the knockout of a steel box?
options: Solvent cement brushed on the threads
A cable tie pulled tight round it
A locknut and a bush, tightened up
A saddle fixed right next to the box

questions.stem: What is an inspection fitting, such as an elbow with a removable cover, used for?
options: To give access for pulling in and checking cables
To let the inspector see the meter readings
To hold the conduit off the wall surface
To join a PVC conduit run to a steel one

questions.stem: Why must every joint in a steel conduit run be tight?
options: So the run does not rattle in the wind
So the conduit stays electrically continuous
So that water can drain out at each joint
So the cables cannot be pulled in later

questions.stem: How is the earth continuity of a finished steel conduit run checked?
options: By looking at the colour of the conduit paint
By tapping each joint lightly with a hammer
With a low-resistance ohmmeter, with all dead
By switching on and touching the conduit

questions.stem: Why should conduit runs be straight, level and parallel to the walls and ceiling?
options: They look neat and are easier to follow later
Straight runs carry more current than bent ones
So that the conduit needs no saddles
So that the code allows a smaller cable

questions.stem: A conduit run is fixed outdoors where it will be rained on. What should be done?
options: Leave the ends of the run open so air can get in
Drill small holes along the top of the run
Use weatherproof fittings, with no water traps
Use thin-wall steel with set-screw couplings

questions.stem: Why must you not put too many cables into one conduit?
options: The conduit will become too heavy for its saddles
Cables may be damaged pulling in and may overheat
The cable colours would be hard to tell apart
The conduit would have to be painted again

questions.stem: Why is a draw wire or draw cord often left in an empty conduit run?
options: So that cables can be pulled in later
So the conduit is earthed without a conductor
To stop insects from getting into the conduit
To hold the conduit straight between saddles

questions.stem: Which is a sign of good conduit workmanship?
options: Bends with flattened, wrinkled outsides
Saddles fitted at uneven gaps along the run
Sharp edges left inside the cut ends
Smooth bends, square cuts and tight joints

questions.stem: Which tool gives a clean, square cut on small PVC conduit without a saw?
options: A sharp cold chisel
Heavy side cutters
A wood block plane
A PVC pipe cutter

questions.stem: Which bend turns a conduit run around a corner, such as from a wall up onto the ceiling?
options: A 90° bend
An offset
A saddle
A coupling

questions.stem: Why are the spare knockouts on a box left closed?
options: So the box can be used again on another job
So the box is lighter and easier to fix
To keep out dust, insects and fingers
So the cable can be pulled in through them

questions.stem: What should be done with short off-cuts of steel conduit after the job?
options: Leave them on the floor for the cleaner
Throw them into the ceiling space
Bury them in the garden outside
Collect them for recycling or the scrap bin

questions.stem: Why is the bare thread on a galvanised steel conduit often painted with zinc-rich paint after threading?
options: To make it the same colour as the box
To protect the bare steel from rust
To make the threads tighter in the coupling
To insulate the conduit from the earth

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters EMT stand for?
What is the name of a single bend of less than 90°, used to move a conduit run away from a surface?
What is the name of the fitting that joins two lengths of conduit in a straight line?
What is the name of the sharp, rough edge left on a conduit after it is cut?
On a hacksaw blade, what do the letters TPI stand for?
Name the vice that holds round conduit firmly while you cut or thread it.
What name is given to the loss of length along a run when an offset is made in it?
Name the tool that marks a long straight line on a wall by snapping a coloured string.
What is the name of the bend made of two 90° bends on one length of conduit, turning the run back on itself in a U shape?
Name the saddle that holds conduit a small distance off the wall surface.
What is the name of the fitting used to join PVC conduit to a threaded box entry or to another type of conduit?
What do the letters PVC stand for?
On a conduit bending machine, what is the curved part that the conduit is bent around called?
What harmful thing is given off if PVC conduit is overheated or burnt?
Name the extra conductor that is often drawn into a steel conduit with the circuit cables, as the code requires.

essays.stem: Describe the hazards when cutting, threading and bending conduit, and say how you would control each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Cut ends and burrs on steel conduit are sharp, so I wear gloves when handling it and ream every cut end. Metal chips and dust can fly into the eyes when sawing, reaming and threading, so I wear safety glasses. Cutting oil and solvent cement can irritate the skin, and solvent cement gives off fumes that can catch fire, so I wear gloves, work where there is good airflow and keep flames away. Heating PVC can scorch it and give off harmful fumes, so I use a heat gun or heating box, never a flame. Bending and carrying long lengths can strain my back and hit people or light fittings, so I lift correctly, get help and watch where the ends go. I check power tools before use, and I fix the pipe vice firmly so the work does not slip.
markingPoints: Sharp ends and burrs: gloves and reaming
Flying chips: safety glasses
Solvent cement and oil: gloves, good airflow, no flames
PVC heating: heat gun or box, never a flame
Manual handling and tools: lift correctly, get help, check tools, secure vice

essays.stem: Describe how to cut and prepare the end of a length of steel conduit so that it is ready to fit.
essays.modelAnswer: I measure the length needed from the drawing and the site, allowing for the fittings, and I measure twice. I mark the cut all the way round the conduit with a marker or a wrap of tape, so the cut will be square. I hold the conduit firmly in a pipe vice, close to the cut. I cut with a hacksaw that has a fine-tooth blade, fitted with the teeth pointing forward and tensioned, using steady full strokes and light pressure; or I use a pipe cutter. Then I ream the inside with a conduit reamer or half-round file to remove the burr, and file the outside edge smooth. If the conduit is to be threaded, I cut the thread with the right die and cutting oil. Finally I clean off chips and oil, and protect any bare thread with zinc-rich paint.
markingPoints: Measures twice, allowing for fittings
Marks the cut square all round and holds the conduit in a pipe vice
Uses a correctly fitted fine-tooth hacksaw or a pipe cutter
Reams the inside and files the outside edge
Threads if needed, cleans, and protects bare thread

essays.stem: Describe how to make a 90° bend in PVC conduit using a bending spring.
essays.modelAnswer: I choose a bending spring that matches the size and type of the conduit, and tie a length of cord to its end so I can pull it out later. I mark the conduit where the bend is to be, measuring from the end as the run needs. I push the spring inside so that its middle is at the bend mark. In cool weather I warm the conduit a little with a heat gun or a warm cloth; in Jamaica's warm weather it often bends cold. I bend the conduit slowly over my knee or a rounded former, spreading the bend so it is smooth and not kinked. I bend it a little past 90°, then ease it back to exactly 90°, and check it with a square. I twist the spring the way that tightens its coils, so it gets thinner, and pull it out with the cord. Finally I check that the bend is round and not flattened.
markingPoints: Chooses the right spring and ties on a cord
Marks the bend and places the middle of the spring there
Bends slowly and smoothly over the knee or a former
Bends slightly past 90°, eases back and checks with a square
Removes the spring by twisting it thinner, and checks for flattening

essays.stem: Describe how to make a 90° bend in steel conduit with a hand bender, so that the bend ends up in the right place.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the bender is the right size for the conduit. I measure from the end of the conduit, or from the last bend, to where the back of the 90° bend must be, and I take away the bender's take-up, as shown on the bender or in the maker's chart. I mark this point on the conduit. I place the conduit in the bender on a firm, flat floor, with the mark lined up with the correct arrow or mark on the bender. I put my foot on the foot pedal to hold the conduit in the shoe, and pull the handle with steady pressure, keeping the conduit flat on the floor. I check with a spirit level or square that the bend is exactly 90°, and that the conduit has not kinked or twisted. Then I measure again to check that the back of the bend is in the right place.
markingPoints: Uses the right size of bender
Measures and takes away the take-up from the maker's marks or chart
Lines up the mark with the bender's mark on a firm floor
Uses foot pressure and a steady pull, keeping the conduit flat
Checks 90°, no kinks or twist, and measures the result

essays.stem: Explain what a saddle bend is, and describe how you would make a three-bend saddle to cross a small pipe on a wall.
essays.modelAnswer: A saddle bend lets a conduit run go over an obstacle, such as a pipe, and then return to the same line on the other side. A three-bend saddle has one centre bend and two smaller outer bends. A common choice is a 45° centre bend with a 22½° bend on each side, so that the run ends up back in line. First I measure the height of the pipe and mark the centre of the pipe on the conduit. I make the centre bend so that it will sit over the middle of the pipe. Then I mark the two outer bends at equal distances on each side, using the bender maker's chart for that pipe height. I make the outer bends in the opposite direction to the centre bend, all in the same flat plane. I check the saddle against the pipe, and with a level, before fixing it.
markingPoints: Saddle goes over an obstacle and returns to the same line
One centre bend and two outer bends (for example 45° and 22½°)
Measures the obstacle and marks its centre on the conduit
Outer bends equal distances each side, opposite direction, same plane
Checks against the pipe and with a level before fixing

essays.stem: Describe how to fix a surface conduit run to a block wall so that it is straight, level and secure.
essays.modelAnswer: I mark the route from the drawing, using a spirit level or laser level for level runs and a plumb bob for vertical drops, and I snap a chalk line. I mark the saddle positions: one close to each box, bend and fitting, and the rest evenly spaced along the run at the distance the code and drawing give. Before drilling, I check for hidden cables and pipes with a detector. I drill the holes with a masonry bit of the right size in a hammer drill, wearing safety glasses, a dust mask and ear protection. I push in wall plugs of the right size and fix the saddles with suitable screws. I fit the conduit so that it sits straight and snug in each saddle, and check it again with the level. Spacer bar saddles can hold the conduit just off the wall where needed.
markingPoints: Marks level and plumb lines and snaps a chalk line
Saddles near every box, bend and fitting, and evenly spaced
Checks for hidden services and wears PPE when drilling
Uses the right drill bit, wall plugs and screws
Checks the finished run is straight, level and snug

essays.stem: Describe how PVC conduit is joined to fittings and boxes, and how steel conduit is joined to steel boxes.
essays.modelAnswer: For PVC, I cut the conduit square and remove any burrs. I make sure the conduit and the socket of the fitting are clean and dry. I apply solvent cement evenly to the outside of the conduit end and the inside of the socket, push the conduit fully home with a slight twist, and hold it for a few seconds while it grips. I wipe off any spare cement and let the joint set before putting any strain on it. I work with good airflow, away from flames, and close the tin after use. For steel conduit, I thread the end or use the right connector. I fit the conduit into the box knockout, tighten a locknut so that it bites into the box, and fit a bush on the inside so the cables have a smooth edge. Screwed couplings must be fully tightened so the run stays electrically continuous.
markingPoints: PVC: square, deburred, clean and dry
PVC: cement on both parts, push fully home with a twist and hold
PVC: good airflow, no flames, let the joint set
Steel: locknut tightened to bite and a bush fitted inside
Steel: couplings fully tight for earth continuity

essays.stem: Compare PVC conduit and steel conduit for a job in a Jamaican home near the sea. Which would you choose, and why?
essays.modelAnswer: Near the sea, the air carries salt, which makes steel rust quickly, even when it is galvanised, especially at cut ends and threads. PVC conduit does not rust or corrode, so it lasts much longer in salty air. PVC is also light, cheap, easy to cut and easy to join with solvent cement, which suits most homes, and it can be fixed on the surface or cast into block walls and concrete. Its weak points are that it can soften in strong heat, it grows and shrinks with the temperature, and it gives no earth path, so a separate earth conductor must always be drawn in. Steel is stronger against knocks, but in a home that strength is rarely needed. I would choose PVC for this job, with expansion couplings on long runs in the sun and an earth conductor in every circuit, as the drawing and code require.
markingPoints: Salt air makes steel rust, even galvanised
PVC does not corrode and is light, cheap and easy to work
PVC limits: heat, expansion, no earth path (separate earth needed)
Steel's extra strength is rarely needed in a home
Chooses PVC with sensible precautions

essays.stem: Describe how you would thread the end of a heavy-gauge steel conduit using a die stock.
essays.modelAnswer: I make sure the end is cut square and reamed, and I hold the conduit firmly in a pipe vice with a short length sticking out. I choose the die that matches the conduit size and thread, fit it in the stock with its tapered lead side facing the conduit, and fit the guide. I put on safety glasses and gloves. I apply cutting oil to the end of the conduit and to the die. I push the die square onto the end and turn it clockwise with steady pressure until it starts to cut. Then I keep turning, adding oil often, and every so often I turn it back a little to break off the metal chips. I stop when the thread is long enough for the coupling or box entry to tighten fully. I turn the die off, clean off the chips and oil, check the thread with a coupling, and protect it with zinc-rich paint.
markingPoints: End cut square and reamed, held in a pipe vice
Correct die fitted the right way round with the guide
Safety glasses, gloves and cutting oil used
Starts square, turns steadily and backs off to clear chips
Correct thread length; cleans, checks with a coupling and protects

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a finished conduit installation before cables are drawn in, and what faults you would look for.
essays.modelAnswer: I compare the installation with the drawing to check that the route, boxes and fittings are in the right places. I check that the runs are straight, level and plumb, and parallel to the walls and ceiling. I look at every bend for kinks, flattening or wrinkles, and at every cut end to make sure it is square and reamed, with no sharp burrs. I check that all couplings and joints are tight and fully home, that PVC joints are properly cemented, and that steel conduit has locknuts and bushes at every box. I check that saddles are fitted near each box and bend and evenly along the runs, and that nothing is loose. I check that inspection fittings and draw-in boxes are where they are needed. For steel, a continuity test is done on the dead system. I report and correct any fault before cables go in.
markingPoints: Checks against the drawing
Runs straight, level, plumb and parallel
Bends free of kinks; ends square and reamed
Joints tight, PVC joints cemented, locknuts and bushes at steel boxes
Saddles correct, access fittings in place, continuity checked, faults reported

practical1.title: Cut, bend and install a PVC conduit run with a 90° bend and an offset
practical1.brief: On a training bay, the group installs a surface run of PVC conduit (20 mm, or the size the assessor gives) from a box at one end, along the wall, through a 90° bend and down to a second box, with an offset to clear a step or batten on the wall, as the assessor's drawing shows. Each member must, while the assessor watches, measure and cut at least one length square, deburr it, and make at least one bend (the 90° bend with a bending spring, or one of the offset bends). The group shares the solvent-cement joints, fixing the boxes and fitting the saddles, so that each member fixes at least two saddles. Pull a draw cord through the finished run. The bay has no cables and no supply. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the run is finished and the area is clean.
materials: PVC conduit (20 mm or as directed), couplings, boxes, saddles and solvent cement
Bending spring to suit the conduit, with a cord tied on
Fine-tooth hacksaw or PVC cutter, and a deburring tool or file
Tape measure, try square, spirit level, plumb bob and chalk line
Hammer drill, masonry bit, wall plugs and screws (or the bay's fixing board)
Heat gun (only if the assessor allows it)
Safety glasses, dust masks, ear protection and gloves
photos: The route marked out with level and plumb lines and saddle positions
A length being cut square and then deburred
The 90° bend made with the spring, checked with a square
The offset, with both bends checked against the step
A solvent-cement joint made into a box or coupling
The finished run, level and plumb, with saddles fitted
The draw cord pulled through the run
The work area cleaned, with off-cuts in the bin
checklist: Measured twice and cut lengths square
Removed all burrs from cut ends
Made a smooth 90° bend with no kinks or flattening, using the spring correctly
Made an offset with equal bends in the same plane
Made solvent-cement joints that are clean, fully home and secure
Fixed saddles near each box and bend and evenly along the run
Run is straight, level and plumb, and matches the drawing
Worked safely and left the area clean and tidy
safety: Wear safety glasses when cutting, drilling and deburring; add a dust mask and ear protection for drilling
Use solvent cement only with good airflow, away from heat and flames; close the tin after use
Never heat PVC with a flame; use a heat gun only if the assessor allows it
Check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling, and use a sound stepladder for high work
The bay has no supply; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Bend and install steel conduit with a 90° bend, an offset and a saddle
practical2.brief: On a training bay, the group installs a run of steel conduit (thin-wall or heavy-gauge, as the assessor gives) between two steel boxes, with a 90° bend, an offset into a box, and a three-bend saddle over a pipe fixed to the bay wall, as the assessor's drawing shows. Each member measures, marks and makes at least one bend on the hand bender while the assessor watches, and cuts and reams at least one end. If heavy-gauge conduit is used, each member also cuts part of a thread with the die stock. Connect the conduit to the boxes with the correct connectors, locknuts and bushes, and fix it with saddles. When it is finished, the group checks the earth continuity of the run from box to box with a low-resistance ohmmeter or multimeter. The bay has no cables and no supply. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Steel conduit, couplings or connectors, steel boxes, locknuts, bushes and saddles
Hand bender (and a die stock with dies and cutting oil, for heavy-gauge conduit)
Hacksaw with a fine-tooth blade or a pipe cutter, conduit reamer and half-round file
Pipe vice, tape measure, marker, spirit level and try square
Hammer drill, masonry bit, wall plugs and screws (or the bay's fixing board)
Safety glasses, gloves, dust masks and ear protection
photos: Conduit held in the pipe vice and cut square
A cut end after reaming, with no burr
A bend mark lined up on the hand bender
The finished 90° bend checked with a square or level
The saddle over the pipe on the wall
A locknut and bush fitted at a box
The continuity check from box to box
The finished run and the clean work area
checklist: Measured and marked bends using the bender's marks and take-up
Cut ends square and reamed every end
Made a 90° bend with no kinks, flattening or twist
Made an offset with equal bends in the same plane, landing in the right place
Made a saddle that clears the pipe and returns the run to its line
Fitted connectors, locknuts and bushes tightly at every box
Fixed saddles near boxes and bends and evenly along the run, level and plumb
Checked earth continuity correctly on the dead run and recorded the reading
safety: Wear safety glasses and gloves when cutting, reaming and threading; cut ends are sharp
Fix the pipe vice firmly, and keep feet and hands clear when bending
Use cutting oil carefully, wipe up spills and wash your hands after use
Check for hidden cables and pipes before drilling, and wear a dust mask and ear protection
The bay has no supply; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
